paras: The Prineville lynching rumor of August 1882 was a report, carried to Albany, Oregon, by a traveler, that a mob at Prineville had lynched five young men from Linn County for stealing horses. Portland dispatches spread the story to California and Nevada papers, but within days the Associated Press agent at The Dalles reported that no lynching had taken place, and the Albany paper that first printed the rumor declared it ill-founded.

On August 11, 1882, the Albany State Rights Democrat reported under the heading "LYNCHED." that it had been rumored the day before that five Linn County boys had been lynched by a mob at Prineville for stealing horses. The paper said the report came from a gentleman who had just arrived from Prineville and called him a reliable source, while adding, "How true it is we do not know as yet." It named the five as John Tharp, Sidney Houston, Emmet Wilson, and two young men named Dinwiddie and Crab; no report gave their race.

Portland dispatches dated August 11 and 12 repeated the rumor, saying it had reached Albany by messenger. On August 14, however, a Portland dispatch relayed word from the Associated Press agent at The Dalles that "no lynching has occurred at Prineville recently."

On August 18 the State Rights Democrat reported that the rumor "has proven to have been ill-founded." The same issue noted that Jos. Blakely, who had left Prineville after the reported time of the lynching, knew nothing of any such affair. The Corvallis Gazette reprinted the retraction in its Linn County column on August 25.

The local paper treated the story cautiously, but the wire versions were less guarded: the Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed it "Rumor of Extensive Lynching," while the Eureka Daily Sentinel ran it as "Five Horse Thieves Lynched." The Seattle Daily Post-Intelligencer carried a "Rumored Lynching" item, and Nevada weeklies including the Silver State and the Lyon County Times reprinted the rumor, with the names garbled in transmission.

The denial traveled less widely than the rumor: on August 26, more than a week after the Albany retraction, the White Pine News stated without qualification that five boys had been lynched at Prineville "on the 12th."

The early reports of a lynching rested on a single traveler's account, while the denial came from the Associated Press agent at The Dalles, from a second traveler, and from the paper that had first printed the rumor, making the denial the stronger evidence. Spellings of the names varied among papers, with Tharp given as Thorp or Thorpe, Emmet Wilson as Earnest Wilson or "Emmet Arlson," and Sidney Houston as "Sydney Hortton."

bases: A rumor that five Linn County young men had been lynched at Prineville for horse stealing (A1, A2, A4) was denied by the Associated Press agent at The Dalles and retracted as ill-founded by the Albany paper that first printed it (A7, A10); no violent episode is established.

The first reports described a mob lynching five men for stealing horses (A1, A2), but the AP agent at The Dalles reported no lynching at Prineville and the originating Albany paper declared the rumor ill-founded (A7, A8, A10); the later, closer reports are the better evidence, so no killing is supported.
Wire reports of a lynching (A1, A2, A4, A13) are contradicted by the AP denial from The Dalles (A7, A8), a traveler from Prineville (A9) and the Albany and Corvallis retractions (A10, A12).
